In January, dozens of new Democratic lawmakers will enter the House of Representatives—many with strong U.S. foreign-policy and national security views.

And while they won’t have the seniority to chair major committees, they could still prove incredibly influential. Just look at the lawmakers who swept in during the last Democratic wave election in 2018 and went on to become household names—figures such as Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Deb Haaland. Some have gone on to win governorships and Senate seats. One—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—is even widely speculated to be considering a high-profile run at the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

It has been revealed that in January, dozens of new Democratic lawmakers will enter the House of Representatives—many with strong U.S. foreign-policy and national security views.

It has been revealed that and while they won’t have the seniority to chair major committees, they could still prove incredibly influential. Just look at the lawmakers who swept in during the last Democratic wave election in 2018 and went on to become household names—figures such as Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Deb Haaland. Some have gone on to win governorships and Senate seats. One—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—is even widely speculated to be considering a high-profile run at the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

Here are five incoming House Democrats who could end up being just as formidable presences in the next Congress, especially on foreign policy and national security.

Industry observers note that retired Army Lt. Col. Fred Wellman rode the blue tsunami to topple a longtime Republican lawmaker. His background as a helicopter pilot with multiple combat tours followed by work in political communications and veterans’ advocacy could position him to be a thorn in the side of the Trump administration and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

In a recent development, wellman served for 22 years in the Army and saw combat four times, including during the first Gulf War and three tours in Iraq. Formerly a lifelong Republican, Wellman switched parties after becoming disgusted with Donald Trump’s disparagement of former Sen. John McCain’s prisoner-of-war status. He would go on to be a veterans’ affairs advisor and later the executive director of the Lincoln Project, a political action committee that drew national attention in the 2020 presidential contest for its acerbic ads that lampooned Trump’s character and record.

It has been revealed that wellman has been a fierce critic of Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran without congressional authorization. He supports continued military assistance to Ukraine and the Block the Bombs Act, legislation popular with progressives that would prohibit the export of some of the United States’ most powerful bombs to Israel.

Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, is another former Republican who flipped a deeply red district. Laubacher narrowly unseated one of MAGA’s most prominent and polarizing House members, Rep. Lauren Boebert, in Colorado’s reddest district.

Laubacher’s distinguished 34-year Navy career, which focused on intelligence matters and South Asia, could propel her to assignments on Capitol Hill’s national security committees, such as House Armed Services or House Intelligence, where her insider knowledge of U.S. surveillance technology and the defense-industrial base bureaucracy is likely to be valued.

In a recent development, in her final years of military service, Laubacher served as defense attaché to India and then on the National Security Council during the Biden administration as the point person for South Asia. During her stint as the top defense official at the U.S. Embassy in Upcoming Delhi, Laubacher was credited with playing an crucial role in facilitating U.S. support for the Indian military during a series of violent 2020 standoffs with the Chinese army along the two countries’ disputed Himalayan border.

Her campaign focused on affordability problems and connecting Trump’s tariff policies and the Iran war to higher cost of living, as well as improving care and services for veterans. She is a member of the Blue Dogs, a caucus of moderate and conservative-leaning House Democrats. Laubacher wants an end to U.S. taxpayer-financed military support for Israel but supports the transfer of weapons to the country on a “case by case basis.”.

Democrats feel they have a mandate to put conditions on U.S. support for Israel.

The world has changed. A new approach must take that into account.

Sources indicate that it wasn’t just Iran. Israel, tariffs, and immigration also loomed large in voters’ minds.

Industry observers note that also hailing from Colorado but from the opposite wing of the Democratic Party is Melat Kiros, a democratic socialist who at 29 years old will become the youngest female lawmaker in Congress in January. Kiros immigrated as a baby with her family from Ethiopia.

Industry observers note that as a junior corporate attorney, she was fired from her job at a prominent law firm for refusing to take down an open letter she published defending law students who expressed pro-Palestinian views in the weeks after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Kiros, who has accused Israel of committing genocide, drew connections to her family’s own experiences, having lost family members to what she called the recent “genocidal war against Tigrayans by the Ethiopian and Eritrean governments.”.

This summer, Kiros successfully challenged from the left the 15-term incumbent progressive lawmaker Rep. Diana DeGette to win the Democratic nomination for the solid blue Denver-area congressional seat. She argued that DeGette and other establishment Democrats had been ineffective in combating Trump. During the primary, Kiros made Israel a distinguishing matter between herself and DeGette. She supports an arms embargo to the country that would cover even defensive systems such as the Iron Dome missile shield.

Recent findings suggest that in the House, Kiros is expected to align with other far-left young progressives such as Ocasio-Cortez. Although Kiros received critical primary campaign backing from the Democratic Socialists of America, she has stated she does not share the national organization’s position that the United States should withdraw from NATO.

Like Kiros, Brad Lander successfully ran to the left of an establishment Democrat in a deep blue district where support for Israel was a key dividing issue. But Lander’s Jewish faith and victory over a pro-Israel incumbent in one of the most Jewish districts in the United States (New York’s 10th) could make him a potent Capitol Hill foil for the Israeli government.

Recent findings suggest that lander, a former New York City councilman and comptroller, is a political ally of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. And he has already been mixing it up online and offline with members of both Israel’s political opposition and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right government. Like many other progressive House Democrats, Lander, whose district includes Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn, supports the Block the Bombs Act.

It has been revealed that when former Israeli Prime Minister Yair Lapid wrote on X shortly after the U.S. midterm elections that his country’s next government should prioritize repairing ties with moderate Democrats in Congress as well as embark on a public relations tour of the United States, Lander pushed back hard.

According to recent reports, “[Y]ou’re not listening to what American voters—Jewish and non-Jewish—are saying,” Lander wrote on X in response. “We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”.

Just a few weeks earlier during a solidarity visit to the West Bank to help Palestinian farmers harvest their olive crop, Lander was detained for several hours by the Israeli military, which remarked it was because his trip presented a “security risk.”.

“Yet one more element of escalating, and very clearly state-sponsored ethnic cleansing,” Lander wrote of the experience.

Speaking of potent foils, Hegseth may face one of his own making when he is eventually called to testify before the House oversight committees.

Nancy Lacore is another retired Navy admiral who narrowly flipped a solidly conservative district in the midterms. But Lacore, who won her South Carolina House seat by just over 3,000 votes, is also one of the highest-ranking officers to be ousted by Hegseth. Her 35-year Navy career, including her most recent position as the chief of the Navy Reserve, would seem to make her a strong candidate for membership on the House Armed Services Committee.

Lacore has remarked she doesn’t know why Hegseth fired her, but she went on to make her opposition to his leadership a central tenet of her campaign. “Pete Hegseth is the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen,” Lacore said in an interview with CBS News after winning election. “He has caused significant damage to us as a country and put us at risk and really damaged the readiness of our entire military force.”.

According to recent reports, the retired three-star vice admiral was a registered Republican until 2016, when Trump became the party’s leader. In January, she will become the highest-ranking female military officer ever to serve in Congress.

  • Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people.
  • According to recent reports, when Salon rolled out in November 1995, the web was a very different place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

According to recent reports, when Salon rolled out in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in latest ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

It has been revealed that the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

In a recent development, the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Sources indicate that thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

The Luxury of Children

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania.
  • Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.
  • The world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania. This piece is adapted from “Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World,” co-authored with Patrick Norrick and forthcoming in the 2027 Annual Review of Economics.

Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.

The world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood. Last year, humanity’s total fertility level dropped below what demographers call the replacement rate—that is, the average number of children that a woman must have to keep a population constant over the long run. This has never happened before. There have been periods when the human population declined because of wars or epidemics, such as the Black Death, in the fourteenth century, or the diseases brought by Europeans to the Americas in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. But now, simply as a function of their choices, humans will see the world population peak around 2055 and then begin to fall.

Sources indicate that the story of the coming decades is not simply one of dwindling and aging. There is a great deal of variation in the baby bust. The most surprising trend may be one that has overturned basic assumptions about fertility rates. Where once it was thought that people—and, by extension, countries—with higher levels of income and education would have lower fertility rates than those who were poorer and less educated, the inverse is increasingly true. Many wealthier people and countries boast higher fertility rates than many poor people and countries.

Recent findings suggest that the inversion is revealing of why governments have had a hard time coming to grips with the fertility crash. The best explanation for why people are no longer having babies is that child-rearing at the scale necessary to maintain populations is fundamentally at odds with the structures of modern life and modern societies. Once an economic necessity, children are now an economic luxury. That portends a world in which economic inequality is accentuated by demographic inequality, with widening fissures within countries and among them. The whole world is grappling with a decline in fertility, but in many different ways. And those differences will stoke further divisions, tensions, and even conflict.

In a recent development, humanity falling below replacement has passed largely unnoticed. The central projections in the latest release of the United Nations World Population Prospects (in 2024), known as the report’s “medium variant,” still places the world’s total fertility rate slightly above replacement in 2026 and expects the global population to peak as late as 2084. But this medium variant does not fully incorporate the recent drops in births recorded by national statistical agencies, and its projections for future fertility rest on questionable assumptions, including forecasting a strong recovery of fertility rates in countries such as China. By comparison, the report’s “low variant” (the forecast that takes a more pessimistic view of future fertility) accords nearly exactly with my own assessment, which reflects more recent national statistics and takes a less optimistic view on the possible recovery of fertility. In that reading, the world has dropped below replacement fertility levels (approximately 2.2 children per woman) and will only keep dropping.

In a recent development, fertility rates are plunging so fast that they are overturning many assumptions about demography. The steepest fertility declines have occurred in unexpected countries. Consider this test. Pick the state with the highest fertility rate among the following: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Jamaica, Iran, Malaysia, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, Sri Lanka, and the United States.

Industry observers note that the United States, the wealthiest of the 12, has the highest fertility rate. This holds true even when just assessing the fertility rate of mothers born in the United States (immigrant mothers have a slightly higher fertility rate than native mothers). Dozens of other middle-income countries now have fertility levels below that of the United States.

According to recent reports, that trend runs against the old explanation for demographic change, which held that fertility invariably falls as a community or society gets richer. That is demonstrably no longer the case. Among the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), richer members tend to have higher fertility rates than do poorer ones, even after controlling for migration flows. Take Mexico. According to the most recent survey, in 2024, a Mexican woman could expect to have 1.2 children over her lifetime, well below the 1.57 average of non-Hispanic white women in the United States. Mexico’s income per capita is only about 28 percent of the U.S. level. And just two decades ago, fertility rates in Mexico were much higher than those in the United States.

In a recent development, this dynamic obtains not just among countries but also within them. Richer and more educated households in the United States and other advanced economies now tend to have more children than poorer and less educated ones, reversing a pattern that had held for centuries.

There is no single, simple answer for why this has happened. Most theories do not hold up against international evidence. Factors that seem to contribute to lower fertility in the United States, for instance, such as higher housing prices, don’t seem to matter elsewhere, as many countries have seen even steeper fertility declines without skyrocketing housing prices.

Recent findings suggest that or take another favorite culprit, smartphones. Some researchers have suggested that the spread of the smartphone stoked atomization and a desire for individual fulfillment, discouraging many people from having children. But fertility rates have been plunging worldwide since the late 1960s, well before smartphones appeared, and there is little evidence of an acceleration in the drop after their introduction. Instead, the device is more likely an accelerator of underlying mechanisms than a cause in itself: by my calculations, smartphones compressed into ten years a change in fertility that would have occurred anyway over 25.

Another common explanation for drops in fertility is the spread of female education and employment. Freed from the domestic function of birthing and raising babies, the argument goes, women have chosen to prioritize other goals instead of child rearing. Although that shift may indeed have played a role in the twentieth century in lowering fertility rates, it is no longer so clearly causal today. Indeed, across OECD countries, the correlation between fertility, on the one hand, and female education and employment, on the other, is positive: the countries where women are more educated and more likely to work outside the home are also the countries with higher fertility rates. And in other regions for which demographers have good vital statistics, such as Latin America, the women not having children in 2026 are the least educated and the ones most likely to not be part of the workforce.

Recent findings suggest that in the absence of neat, definitive explanations, a broader explanation for the global fertility crash comes into view. As societies embrace what is often termed “modernity,” they become incapable of maintaining replacement-level fertility rates. Modernity describes how countries have organized contemporary life around formal institutions (such as schools, universities, and health systems), specialized expertise (through degree accreditation, standardized exams, and professional licensing), and large-scale systems of coordination (such as multinational corporations, governments, and global supply chains). It is not synonymous with capitalism; communist countries, too, invested heavily in mass education and bureaucracies (and saw concomitant declines in fertility). The only way to run large, complex societies that harness modern technology at scale is to standardize knowledge and detach it from local custom through mass education, systems of expertise, and bureaucracies.

Modernity raises the cost of children and lowers the cost of childlessness. Parents must equip children with formal knowledge and credentials, an endeavor that takes decades of effort and spending. Tight career schedules also conflict with parents’ biological clocks. The most productive years for a research economist, for example, are usually between 30 and 45. Those are also the years when one needs to spend the most time with children. No matter how much accommodation a university offers, the day still has only 24 hours. Even when a researcher manages to produce both a large family and strong academic output, one can always wonder how much more that researcher would have produced with a smaller family.

And modernity has also made it easier not to have children. In traditional agrarian and artisan economies, children were useful factors of production, helping in the fields and workshops. Children also provided parents and other older relatives with eldercare. But the modern organization of economic life no longer requires children to perform those roles and the advent of welfare states has given the elderly other forms of support. Lineage once determined people’s present and future; it no longer does so in such a comprehensive way.

It has been revealed that there are some exceptions to this seemingly universal trend. Tight-knit religious communities, such as the ultra-Orthodox in Israel and the Amish in the United States, have managed to maintain high fertility rates well above replacement level. But these groups have also stayed apart from much of modern life. For example, the Amish live in rural areas, where housing is much cheaper, and they end formal education at eighth grade, which eliminates one of the main costs of raising a child in a modern society, advanced education.

It has been revealed that apart from these idiosyncratic pockets, modernity has spread around the planet, with fertility falling everywhere. But rates are tumbling unevenly. In 1980, the richer an OECD country, the fewer children its women had. By 2000, the opposite was beginning to become true. The same reversal demonstrates up inside countries. In Sweden, the demographer Martin Kolk has found that in every cohort born between 1940 and 1970, men with higher lifetime incomes have more children, and that among women born since the 1960s, the poorest have the fewest children. In the United States, the economists Moshe Hazan and Hosny Zoabi have found that in the first decade of the twenty-first century, women with a graduate degree had about 2.0 children, significantly more than the 1.8 for women who stopped at a bachelor’s degree.

Industry observers note that many adults still want to have children and flourishing families. When Gallup asked Americans about their ideal number of children in July 2025, the average answer was 2.7, a figure that has barely changed since the 1970s. But children are costly and bring no income. They have become something of a luxury good that richer people can afford more of than poorer people can. In the same way that a richer household owns, on average, a more expensive car than a poorer one, it also has more children—at least since the 1990s. Prosperous parents can hire help at home, order prepared meals, pay for premium grocery delivery or laundry services, and afford tuition and tutoring.

Richer families (and, among them, the most educated parents) also have more stable family lives. For instance, among Americans born between 1957 and 1964 (a cohort whose adult lives can be observed almost in full), about half of men with a high school diploma but no college education had seen their first marriage end in divorce by age 55, compared with 27 percent of men with a bachelor’s degree or more. Stable families lead to higher fertility (and much better outcomes for the children). In short, income and education soften some of the worst consequences of modernity. The intuition of this result applies, as well, to countries as a whole: richer countries can, on average, afford more “luxuries,” including children, than poorer countries.

Industry observers note that if the modernity conjecture is right, the flip in the correlation between income and fertility that is evident within OECD countries will extend to all other countries over the next few decades. This is already happening in the Americas: among countries with at least 20 million inhabitants, the United States has the highest fertility rate in the hemisphere, well ahead of Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, and Mexico, and matched only by Peru, whose fertility rate is plummeting fast. (Venezuela’s official fertility rate is pure fiction.).

The same phenomenon will occur in sub-Saharan Africa over the next few decades. It is often projected that the continent’s high fertility rates will make up for shortfalls elsewhere—but that will likely not happen. Indeed, in those sub-Saharan African countries for which demographers have slightly better statistical data, fertility rates are dropping very promptly. For example, a recent household survey in the Republic of Congo has shown a decrease in fertility from 5.1 children per woman in 2011–12 to 3.5 in 2025. Similar falls are happening elsewhere and likely to accelerate as sub-Saharan Africa succumbs to the same factors that have sped fertility declines elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that the coming years will produce deep changes in populations within countries and across countries. The already sharp divide between regions and social groups with higher average incomes and education levels and those with lower average incomes and education levels will grow more pronounced, with the added dimension of contrasting fertility rates. The school district of a wealthy suburb outside a major East Coast city may not need to grapple with the widespread school closings that urban districts are already experiencing. And since political power in a democracy follows, at least to some extent, the number of voters, these different regions and social groups will see their relative influence in American politics change: Newly introduced York, for instance, has lost 19 votes in the electoral college since the 1940s.

It has been revealed that something similar can happen among countries. In 1972, nearly eight times as many children were born in China as in the United States. In 2025, that figure has dropped to 2.2 times as many. China’s total fertility rate in 2025 was 0.93, while the U.S. rate was 1.58. If fertility rates remain at those levels, the United States will overtake China in annual births at some point in the 2080s and in total population by around 2120. That date might arrive earlier if the gap between the fertility rates of China and the United States continues to widen.

It has been revealed that demography is not necessarily destiny, but a world in which the United States has a larger population than China is very different from the world today. The shrinking and aging of populations will have first-order effects on a country’s economic performance. In research with Gustavo Ventura and Wen Yao, I have documented that nearly all of Japan’s poor economic performance relative to the United States since 1990 can be explained by its worse demographics, not by financial crises or poor economic policy. Among the great powers, the United States is the least exposed to demographic headwinds. Younger populations tend to be more innovative and less reliant on public support, a fact that bodes well for American prospects in the competition to come.

But for most other countries, demographic decline will produce significant problems. Aging Japan, for instance, is likely the best-case scenario for countries reaching a demographic sunset. It boasts a capable state and a homogeneous society with a high degree of consensus. More important, Japan became rich before it got old. Countries such as Mexico and Thailand, which lack many of Japan’s advantages, may struggle to weather the same demographic headwinds. While rich economies can rely on immigration to soften some of the effects of falling fertility, countries such as Tunisia or Bolivia, which lose many people to emigration, may find it harder to deal with their own baby busts. The new dynamics of fertility augur a world in which gaps between the haves and the have-nots grow even wider, as poorer countries and communities endure strains that wealthier countries and communities manage to escape.

Short of an unlikely turn to the social mores of deeply conservative and ideological communities, such as the Amish, only transformations in material circumstances will help raise fertility rates. Governments have had a hard time determining how to tackle fertility decline. Policy can do only so much in convincing people to make the monumental decision to have children. But that does not mean that governments should not try to reverse these trends. Their policies should respect the freedom of citizens to form the families they believe are best for them. Ultralow fertility seems to be caused not by a lack of desire for children but by the absence of the conditions that would make having children easier, or even possible.

In this vein, some policies are no-brainers. Governments should make education systems more accessible and less competitive than, for example, the ones found in East Asia and in the United States, where high levels of cost and stress discourage having children. They should build more affordable housing and provide more affordable childcare. Such material changes may have only a marginal impact on rates, but even, for instance, raising the U.S. total fertility rate to 1.7 from the current 1.58 would produce a significant impact. Fertility rates behave like the rates of return on a retirement fund: small yearly differences accumulate into large differences over time. Policies that give people greater material freedom to have children can thus be very consequential in the long term.

In a recent development, if governments fail to enact these policies, and if, indeed, these policies fail to encourage a broader rise in fertility, the world will simply become more unequal. Richer families and richer countries will gain greater weight in the population, while poorer families and poorer countries dwindle and weaken. These shifts will create political tensions, as shrinking populations will add to their relative poverty the desperate sense that they have no demographic future. Eastern Germany offers a preview. Since reunification, its young people (above all, its young women) have left for western Germany, its towns have emptied and aged, and its voters have turned to the parties at both extremes of the political spectrum. Many countries in the world are about to become eastern Germany, but few of them will have a western Germany to pay the bills. Demographers often suggest that the world is united by the crash in fertility rates. In truth, demographic decline will likely divide the world even further.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia’s bridge to Crimea.

Industry observers note that U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

In a recent development, welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia’s bridge to Crimea.

Sources indicate that U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

China, however, may have already beaten Trump to the punch.

It has been revealed that right out of the gate, Chinese President Xi Jinping has signaled that his administration is willing to act as a counterweight to the White House’s increasingly provocative trade policies. On Tuesday, Beijing agreed to cut duties on a swath of Canadian exports, amounting to roughly $280 million in tariff relief. In exchange, Ottawa promised to extend remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by another two years.

“Stronger communication and cooperation between China and Canada will benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world,” Xi told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during talks in Shenzhen, China. This was their third meeting since Carney took power in 2025, and it marked Ottawa’s continued efforts to diversify its trade away from Washington.

China also pledged on Tuesday to provide Peru with $22.5 million in aid to address what is expected to be the devastating fallout of this year’s El Niño. Lima applauded the measure, with President Keiko Fujimori stressing that “China is very vital to us because it is our ​principal trading partner.”.

In a recent development, peru is one of the many places in Latin America where Beijing and Washington have competed for influence. Earlier this month, the U.S. State Department disclosed that it has committed $4.5 million to help Peru modernize its main port at Callao, in a move seen as a direct counter to a Chinese-controlled megaport less than 50 miles away that opened in 2024.

Perhaps most notably, though, is China’s potential openness to converse with Japan. A war of words over Taiwan, coupled with Beijing’s rare-earth export controls, has plagued Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s tenure. However, during Tuesday’s ASEAN gathering in Manila, Takaichi shook hands with Chinese Agriculture Minister Zhang Zhu. Although few words were exchanged, the fact that such an interaction occurred has raised hopes that Takaichi’s upcoming trip to Shenzhen may be more cordial than previously anticipated.

In a recent development, yet Beijing’s biggest days may still be to come. On Wednesday, Xi will host Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for trilateral talks on nuclear disarmament and the Iran war. With Trump at his weakest point to date (entering his lame-duck term after sweeping midterm losses and a Nvidia spy scandal), experts anticipate that Xi will aim to capitalize on Trump’s rocky footing.

“Trump is liable to make large and unwise concessions to his imagined peers in order to secure political coups that he hopes can restore prestige and momentum to his badly weakened presidency,” FP columnist Howard W. French argued.

Recent findings suggest that dirty bomb threat? Iran is actively planning for potential strikes on U.S. soil, seven U.S. officials told CNN on Tuesday. Whether Tehran will or even can execute such an attack is unclear, and White House spokesperson Lauren Bis has insisted that “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Still, even the possibility of such an assault signals growing alarm that a peaceful end to the Iran war may be out of reach.

CNN reported that, according to U.S. intelligence, Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. Sources told CNN that this is not an indicator of an imminent attack but rather is one of several options that Iran may be exploring. Iranian officials, however, denied the report, with chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf calling it “false flags” and “war mongering.”.

Industry observers note that experts, meanwhile, insist that Tehran may not have the capabilities or the desire to carry out such a plot. “An Iranian dirty bomb in Washington would be very hard to pull off,” retired U.S. Navy Adm. James Stavridis told CNN. “They’d have to move uranium halfway around the world and have a team in place to set it off. I don’t think they’ll do it. The U.S. response would be overwhelming.”.

In a recent development, trump expressed a similar notion on Tuesday. When asked about the CNN article, the U.S. president told reporters that Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” were it to attack the United States homeland.

Crosshairs on Crimean bridge. Ukrainian forces launched a second strike on Tuesday at a strategic bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014. “Russia built a myth around it as a symbol of Crimea being ‘Russian forever,’” Ukraine’s military command said in a statement. “Now, part of the structure lies in the water.” The attack marked the second consecutive assault on the critical crossing in just two days.

The Kerch Strait Bridge—often highlighted as one of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects—is the only rail crossing between Russia and the Crimean territory. Moscow has repeatedly used the 12-mile road to transport military and civilian supplies to its troops as well as to exert control over Ukraine’s southern coast; the Kerch Strait acts as a chokepoint for naval access from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov. In recent years, the route has also become a symbol of Russia’s yearslong occupation.

In a recent development, ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky characterized this week’s attacks on the bridge as the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes. Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed on Tuesday that the assault on Kerch Strait Bridge occurred in tandem with a massive Ukrainian drone operation; Moscow claimed to have intercepted 1,441 drones across 22 regions on Tuesday in one of Kyiv’s biggest such attacks yet.

What is Belgrade’s future? Hundreds of people gathered outside Serbia’s National Assembly on Tuesday to cheer on the country’s new parliament, the first since the ouster of President Aleksandar Vucic. Led by the grassroots Student List movement, the inaugural session kicked off what is expected to be the long process of forming a government.

According to recent reports, nearly two years of student-led protests against one of Europe’s most staunchly populist regimes culminated in the opposition’s sweeping victory in parliamentary elections last month. Student List lawmakers dominated in the polls, winning 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly compared to the Vucic-led Serbian Progressive Party’s 103 seats. Vucic initially blamed foreign interference for his loss, without citing evidence, despite international observers noting that his party held an unfair advantage.

Now begins the difficult task of governing a country that has been led by Vucic for the past 14 years. On Tuesday, the Student List was expected to nominate university professor Aleksandar Cupic to be the country’s new parliamentary speaker. After that, the grassroots movement will still have to choose a prime minister and hold a snap presidential election; the deadline for the latter expires at the end of this year.

It has been revealed that the end of Pope Leo XIV’s 12-day Latin America tour wrapped up this week with a painful surprise. While traveling in the popemobile before his final Mass in Peru on Monday, Leo was struck in the eye by a flying rosary. It is unclear who threw the prayer beads, as worshippers often toss gifts at the pope, who is known for his (usually) quick reflexes.

Industry observers note that however, Leo has already shaken off the incident. “The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart—or maybe in your eye—but that mark the life of someone,” Leo said on Tuesday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

Recent findings suggest that “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., noted earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

Sources indicate that “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., stated during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

In a recent development, “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” stated panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

Industry observers note that the committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she remarked in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

Industry observers note that “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack mentioned in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., remarked everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he noted at Thursday’s meeting.

#6712. Latest Update: China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2467 w)

Latest Update: China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2467 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Upcoming American Security.
  • Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI?
  • Industry observers note that beijing has long appreciated this dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Upcoming American Security. He served as AI Policy Coordinator in the Office of the Special Envoy for Critical and Emerging Technology at the State Department from 2023 to 2025.

And America Should Be Taking Notes.

Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI? That is the question driving debates in Washington about the wisdom of pursuing talks on the subject with Beijing. The Biden administration paired sweeping technology restrictions with a narrow dialogue on risk, and the Trump administration has kept a channel open even as it has downplayed safety. Some experts go further. They hope that cooperation on safety can be siloed off from competition entirely, a belief as appealing as it is fanciful. Any dialogue on AI risk takes place within the broader strategic competition between the United States and China.

Industry observers note that beijing has long appreciated this dynamic. Much of Washington has not. Whereas the United States has shifted its approach to AI competition and safety across and within presidential administrations, Beijing has kept its AI diplomacy focused on gaining competitive advantage over the United States. China has taken part in international AI safety discussions, but it has used them, along with talks with the United States, to paint U.S. export controls as the main obstacle to cooperation. It has cast itself as the champion of the developing world, promising a Chinese-led AI ecosystem without technological or financial barriers as an alternative to a restrictive U.S.-led AI order. The pitch is working. A growing number of states are embracing China’s message, and Chinese open-weight models are gaining people across the developing world.

If the United States wants to maintain its lead and make meaningful progress on safety, it needs to treat the dialogue as part of the competition with China. To do so, it must ramp up pressure on China outside the talks and offer countries still choosing sides a more compelling vision for AI adoption and governance. And when U.S. and Chinese officials next meet, in November, Washington should test Beijing’s seriousness about safety. In short, the United States should approach AI diplomacy with the same strategic clarity China has.

The Biden administration’s first round of advanced semiconductor export controls in October 2022 and the release of ChatGPT a month later signaled that the United States had taken an early lead in the AI competition and would act to weaken China’s AI industry. Washington and its allies also seized the diplomatic initiative, taking the first steps toward global AI governance. In May 2023, the G-7 began intense discussions on AI governance that would eventually produce a code of conduct for developers. Weeks later, the United Kingdom announced it would host the first global AI safety summit at Bletchley Park.

Recent findings suggest that china responded by rolling out a diplomatic script it has been honing ever since. Its core tenets first appeared in the Global AI Governance Initiative, published in October 2023. It called for countries to “put equal emphasis on development and security” (though it left security to be defined by individual states) and contrasted China’s focus on cooperation and development with U.S. export controls, attacking Washington for “creating barriers and disrupting the global AI supply chain through technological monopolies and unilateral coercive measures.” Despite Beijing’s growing body of AI regulations at home, the initiative offered little more than slogans on the technology’s risks.

That basic formula—cooperation and development, set against U.S. restrictions, with little to say about risk—has guided China’s AI diplomacy for the last three years. In March 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a U.S.-led resolution on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI intended to appeal to both developed and developing countries. China supported the resolution, then introduced another resolution centered on help for poorer countries and “emphasizing that member states should enjoy equal opportunities” to develop and use AI. At a UN Security Council meeting on AI chaired by the United States in December that year, China’s UN ambassador, Fu Cong, once again counterposed Beijing’s stated interest in cooperation against “discriminatory barriers based on ideological differences.” In thinly veiled terms, Fu was charging that U.S. restrictions on China harmed the developing world.

In a recent development, to win the support of these countries as they built out their AI infrastructure, China needed a bloc of its own. In July 2025, Premier Li Qiang proposed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which promised developing countries technology, training, and a greater say in writing global AI rules. In a speech marking its launch a year later, Chinese leader Xi Jinping called for “openness,” shorthand for access to U.S. chips and the adoption of Chinese open-weight models. After urging countries to take the risks of AI seriously, Xi added that they should, “in the meantime,” jointly oppose “overstretching the national security concept in the field of AI and placing one country’s security over that of others.” Cooperation on risks, in Xi’s telling, was subordinate to overcoming U.S. restrictions.

It has been revealed that WAICO has quickly gained standing among its target audience. An early endorsement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres lent it immediate credibility in the eyes of developing countries, and Chinese officials have since promoted WAICO in frequent speeches and in bilateral meetings with countries as varied as Brazil, Pakistan, and Serbia. Beijing has signaled that membership will come with perks. Its draft export controls on leading models, released in October, promise to help WAICO’s 37 members build their AI capabilities, suggesting members could have easier access to models restricted for the rest of the world.

Xi personally led this diplomatic offensive in the lead-up to the Washington summit with U.S. President Donald Trump in September. During a speech in Kyrgyzstan, he pledged to expand a Chinese AI center for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization that helps members build local language models and train engineers. In Cairo, he and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi signed agreements on AI, data centers, and semiconductors, which have become a staple of Xi’s trips abroad. And in New Delhi, Xi proposed an open-source AI zone for BRICS members and told other leaders that a “small yard, high fences” approach would only “box oneself in and divide the world.” AI risks were nowhere on the agenda. The message instead was that U.S. restrictions would isolate Washington, not Beijing.

Much of the allure of China’s pitch rests on how the country’s developers share their technology. Chinese developers release their best models with open weights, which any government or organization can download, run on its own hardware, and adapt to its own language. For governments wary of depending on American companies whose exports Washington can restrict, open-weight models promise a greater degree of control. Chinese developers rarely conduct or publish the results of any safety testing for these models, leaving others to discover after release whether, for example, they can be used to launch cyberattacks or build weapons. But their accessibility allows Beijing to argue that any effort to contain the risks of Chinese models is an attempt to deny AI to the developing world.

Sources indicate that china’s approach to bilateral AI talks with the United States has deflected discussions of risk just as assiduously as its global AI diplomacy has. In May 2024, the United States and China held talks in Geneva, which I joined as part of the U.S. delegation. The U.S. objective of the talks was to test whether an in-depth technical exchange with China on AI risk was possible. The answer was no. Chinese diplomats steered the discussion away from risks for hours and declined to even explain China’s own AI regulations beyond a superficial overview, despite having technical experts from the relevant agencies in the room.

The Chinese position came through most clearly in the opening and closing remarks of the delegation’s most senior officials. They began with an appeal for cooperation on capacity-building projects in the developing world. They then cast U.S. technology restrictions as an attempt to contain China’s development and the U.S. emphasis on safety as a barrier preventing developing countries from accessing and using AI. The implication was clear—export controls were the primary impediment to cooperation on AI safety. The one concrete outcome, a November 2024 statement in which former President Joe Biden and Xi affirmed “the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons,” asked little of Beijing.

This September, after the summit between Trump and Xi in Washington, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs published an “eight-point consensus,” Beijing’s account of what the two sides had agreed to. It described the dialogue as an exchange on the “risks and benefits” of AI. But whereas the White House framed the dialogue as a security problem, listing it alongside nuclear arms control, China’s Ministry of Commerce stressed instead that talks had taken place, and would continue, under the two countries’ economic and trade mechanism. Folded into trade talks, a dialogue on AI risks and benefits leaves Beijing free to parry U.S. requests on risks, such as limits on openly releasing models with dangerous capabilities, by demanding that Washington relax export controls.

Xi did propose to “jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” conveniently eliding China’s own frequent use of AI against the United States in various ways, such as hacking campaigns and influence operations. He added that AI should remain under human control and be developed for good, a principle Beijing has repeated since 2023 but about which it has offered little further detail or follow-through. More pointed was his insistence that future dialogue should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” and his request that Chinese companies be “treated fairly,” both implicit rebukes of U.S. restrictions.

Sources indicate that this record suggests Beijing will come to future meetings, beginning with the next discussion in November, with proposals designed to put Washington in a bind. Although U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has made clear that export controls are not on the table, Beijing will raise them anyway. If Washington engages, Chinese negotiators will claim a standing channel where U.S. restrictions on AI technology are up for negotiation. If it refuses, Beijing will continue to evade U.S. entreaties on safety while accusing Washington of stifling opportunity for developing countries. It hopes that every round of the dialogue will further cement an impression among allies such as Japan and the Netherlands that Washington will trade away restrictions over their heads, and that they should accommodate China’s AI ambitions, too.

But Washington is in a stronger position than its diplomacy has let on. The world’s leading models are still American, and, together with allies, the United States controls key chokepoints in the semiconductor supply chain. Export controls on those chokepoints are not a bargaining chip and should be strengthened. Chinese AI companies regularly lament their lack of high-end chips and have resorted to smuggling chips and illicitly distilling U.S. models. U.S. developers also conduct increasingly extensive and transparent safety testing, which Chinese developers avoid. Taken together, these strengths give Washington the means to press Beijing and an attractive offer for the rest of the world. It should use them, advertising its rigorously tested models to compete for global adoption while pressuring China on safety in the dialogue.

According to recent reports, the first chance to apply that pressure is the next bilateral meeting. Washington should set two conditions for it and future meetings. Chinese developers must commit to publishing safety evaluations at least as extensive as those that leading U.S. developers publish today on equivalent benchmarks for the most serious risks, such as cyberattacks and biological weapons, and to disclosing previous and future incidents. The United States can make the same commitments, as its companies already publish such evaluations, increasingly disclose incidents, and open their models to independent and government evaluators before release. Otherwise, the incident channel to which the two sides agreed in September will run one way, with China free to point to U.S. incidents while reporting none of its own.

These conditions would change the terms of the dialogue. Since 2023, Washington has raised risks and Beijing has steered the conversation toward development. As long as Chinese companies face no scrutiny for the risks of their models, Beijing can tout them for their openness and innovation without having to answer questions from the rest of the world about their safety. Concordia AI, which tracks China’s AI ecosystem, found that only five of China’s ten leading developers published safety test results for any model over the past year, and none did so consistently. If China agrees, governments and companies choosing which models to use will be able to judge Chinese and American developers by the same criteria. If China refuses, the onus will be on Beijing to explain why fair treatment for Chinese companies should not extend to safety testing. Regardless, the U.S. government should ramp up its own tests of newly introduced Chinese models and publish the results. It should also avoid unforced errors, such as Trump’s waving away of AI safety concerns as a “hoax,” which hand Beijing an easy retort to U.S. appeals.

More broadly, effective AI diplomacy ultimately requires convincing other countries to join the American AI ecosystem. Countries that train their engineers, build their local language models, and run their data centers on Chinese technology will come to depend on it. To counter that dependence (and prevent it from turning into political alignment), Washington needs to present a positive vision of AI governance that pairs verifiable safety commitments—the kind Chinese developers avoid—with the access and investment developing countries want.

U.S. companies already offer the best technology, but Washington has yet to put real diplomatic weight behind them. It should draw from its evolving approach at home to rally partners around shared safety measures. Under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, six leading U.S. companies committed themselves to internal controls, external audits, and independent oversight. The G-7 Code of Conduct, which built on voluntary commitments secured under the Biden administration, could incorporate the accord’s measures and serve as a common standard for partners. Countries that agree to its measures could receive priority for technology and financing. Without such incentives, the AI competition may be determined by price and access alone, where China has the edge.

According to recent reports, much of Washington has treated talks with Beijing as a place to manage the shared risks of AI apart from the competition. China has always treated them as an arena of the larger rivalry. To maintain its lead and make real progress on safety, the United States should start doing the same.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside. He also turned down the negotiated package on the table. Instead, he chose to keep tightening the screws on Iran through an economic blockade. Yet, rumors that he has shelved the military option or is warming to a deal are hasty. The more probable outcome is that he neither ends the conflict nor resolves it, but quietly drifts away from it while gradually loosening the blockade on Iran.

In a recent development, pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that several factors will limit Trump’s ability to resume military action against Iran. First, Netanyahu may have only a few weeks left as Israel’s caretaker. If Gadi Eisenkot succeeds in forming a government in the next few weeks, Netanyahu will lose the premiership and his long-term dream of crushing the Iranian state. A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside. He also turned down the negotiated package on the table. Instead, he chose to keep tightening the screws on Iran through an economic blockade. Yet, rumors that he has shelved the military option or is warming to a deal are hasty. The more probable outcome is that he neither ends the conflict nor resolves it, but quietly drifts away from it while gradually loosening the blockade on Iran.

According to recent reports, pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that several factors will limit Trump’s ability to resume military action against Iran. First, Netanyahu may have only a few weeks left as Israel’s caretaker. If Gadi Eisenkot succeeds in forming a government in the next few weeks, Netanyahu will lose the premiership and his long-term dream of crushing the Iranian state. A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a newly introduced government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.

Second, in two months’ time, Trump’s maneuverability will be eclipsed by a Democratic Congress that can defund the war. Third, though U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment attempt last week, his political future still hangs by a thread.

Industry observers note that even if the risk of war declines, this does not guarantee a greater likelihood of a deal. Key obstacles—including Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile, the future of its enrichment program, a regional cease-fire, sanctions relief, and the political cost for Trump—make both reaching and maintaining an agreement challenging.

The most likely scenario may turn out to be neither war nor peace, yet something altogether different from the economic blockade “middle path” that Trump chose earlier. In this scenario, Trump’s economic warfare and blockade would end up little more than words on paper. Trump would declare victory, reject both war and peace, withdraw the U.S. military, step away from the table, and insist that the blockade and sanctions remain in place while quietly allowing them to fade into irrelevance.

This would set in motion a gradual loosening of the blockade, with sanctions enforcement quietly eroding. Bit by bit, Asian and Middle Eastern countries would ramp up trade and investment in Iran, far surpassing current levels. Out of this slow transformation, a delicate latest equilibrium would take shape: Sanctions enforcement would remain just robust enough for the United States to insist the system is intact, yet lax enough to persuade Tehran not to upset the emerging status quo.

It has been revealed that this Swiss-cheese scenario is the only walk-away option that could work. If Trump truly keeps the blockade and sanctions in place, then the United States and Iran would be locked in a relentless standoff, always teetering on the edge of conflict, just as they are now. This fragile balance would inevitably tip into another war, completely undermining the whole point of walking away.

To be clear, the Swiss-cheese scenario is suboptimal compared with a peace deal. A peace deal that would end 47 years of enmity, uphold nonproliferation goals, open the Iranian economy to U.S. companies, and stabilize the region would far better serve U.S. interests. But the walk-away option carries the benefit, from Trump’s perspective, of avoiding an agreement that would manifest the failure of his war, as the Islamabad Memorandum did in the view of its critics. He will find it attractive because his focus is no longer on how much he can get, but how much he can avoid giving.

Indeed, the Swiss-cheese option guarantees that, while none of the sides walks away with a complete victory, everyone sidesteps their worst nightmare. Trump escapes both a humiliating compromise and the quagmire of another needless war. Tehran, in turn, dodges the devastation that a joint U,S. and Israeli assault on its vital infrastructure and energy lifelines would unleash. And given the shift in favor of nuclear weapons among the Iranian public, Iranian decision-makers may also welcome de facto partial sanctions relief without having to give up their stockpile of enriched uranium or give other nuclear concessions.

Even Israel might breathe easier, since its worst fear—a U.S.-Iran diplomatic breakthrough that could see old enemies reconcile—remains off the table, while the possibility of a future U.S.-Iran conflict still lingers. Israeli leaders will certainly view any loosening of the sanctions pressure as a loss, but it is still superior to a deal that undoes the sanctions architecture altogether. Moreover, Israel may calculate that the scenario still offers plenty of opportunities to tighten the sanctions or even escalate matters toward war.

In short, it’s neither side’s worst option, and everyone’s least-costly scenario.

And while Israel may still hope for chances to escalate, the Swiss-cheese scenario could turn out to be unexpectedly resilient, even as it leaves the U.S.-Iran conflict unresolved. Should this uneasy balance persist until 2029, the next U.S. president will stand at a crossroads: reignite tensions in pursuit of a better deal or quietly embrace the status quo and turn attention to the many other pressing crises on the United States’ plate. To most presidents, this will be a rather simple choice.

Given Trump’s refusal to admit defeat, his dread of looking like a loser, his allergy to tangled diplomacy, his fixation on eclipsing former U.S. President Barak Obama’s Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, and Iran’s refusal to offer him an ego-saving escape, Trump may ultimately declare a false victory and settle for the Swiss-cheese walk-away—not because it’s the smarter move but because it’s the cheapest way out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, remarked additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, the Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

“When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

Industry observers note that last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they noted they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

It has been revealed that on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

Industry observers note that “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

“When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet noted in a statement.

Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

It has been revealed that “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., noted Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

It has been revealed that the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.
