📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

And Now He Needs a New Strategy.

Recent findings suggest that stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery.

Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump unveiled that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”.

Industry observers note that trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

Recent findings suggest that if leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

For a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

In a recent development, although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

In a recent development, since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

Even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the upcoming memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

Still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

Russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most crucial partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the concern. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s newly introduced approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

Sources indicate that whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

The Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

Although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a new opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

Three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same concern that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

It has been revealed that one possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

Recent findings suggest that kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

In a recent development, in the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

To ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

Although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

It has been revealed that regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

Sources indicate that finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

Recent findings suggest that if North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a upcoming campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

Recent findings suggest that beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as notable: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

In a recent development, even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

Any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

Industry observers note that despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

Sources indicate that trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

The bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the issue, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

Recent findings suggest that growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a latest world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

But this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.

Industry News: Cooperating With China on AI Control Is a Fantasy

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Should the United States slow down artificial intelligence development to address possible existential risks to humanity?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In a recent development, should the United States slow down artificial intelligence development to address possible existential risks to humanity? The Trump administration prefers a “let it rip” approach to winning the AI race. But a growing chorus of American tech titans want to slow down AI development so that risk prevention measures can catch up with the technology.

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, for example, argued that “we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” He calls for “building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman posted on X, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”.

Should the United States slow down artificial intelligence development to address possible existential risks to humanity? The Trump administration prefers a “let it rip” approach to winning the AI race. But a growing chorus of American tech titans want to slow down AI development so that risk prevention measures can catch up with the technology.

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, for example, argued that “we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” He calls for “building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits and grappling with key geopolitical dilemmas.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman posted on X, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”.

However, the case for greater controls contains a major weakness: It rests on coordination with China. Amodei’s three-point strategy for pacing AI, for example, will require “cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities.”.

According to recent reports, altman agreed. He stated, “Even if just the U.S. and China could agree on some shared standards and testing for development of this technology, I think that’d be a wonderful accomplishment that the two of them can deliver.”.

Jacob Coxon, who made international news when he resigned from Anthropic in September, remarked, “A race with China could be very bad and that we should be taking pretty rapid actions for international coordination.”.

It has been revealed that but coordinating with China is much easier stated than done. Chinese President Xi Jinping is not interested in negotiating controls on AI development, and even if he were, he could not be trusted to abide by them. Believing that we can work with Beijing is a tech-world fantasy rooted in a shallow understanding of geopolitics.

To be fair, Amodei wrote, “We must not be naïve here: the geopolitical stakes are so high that there will likely be stark limits on what can be achieved.” But he and other technologists do not seem to fully grasp the depth of the challenge. Washington cannot afford, therefore, to unilaterally restrain itself as Beijing races ahead.

Just like with Cold War-era nuclear arms control agreements, any AI restraints must be mutually binding and verifiable. But Beijing is not interested in negotiating binding restraints. Instead, Xi has criticized Western attempts to control AI. China’s AI diplomacy instead trumpets the technology’s potential for economic development, especially for the global south.

In response to Amodei’s proposals for coordinated controls, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated that “fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance.”.

Moreover, China and other dictatorships might even have rational incentives to embrace—not control—AI applications that court catastrophic risk. They trust algorithms more than their own people. Humans do not always reliably carry out orders, but computers do. I’ve talked to experts who say that China’s military officers, for example, are worryingly optimistic about the benefits and controllability of AI-enabled weapons systems.

It has been revealed that further, even if Washington and Beijing could agree on mutual constraints, Beijing is unlikely to abide by them. Dictatorships in general—and China, in particular—tend to cheat on international agreements. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union regularly cheated on nuclear arms control agreements while dictatorships like Iran, Iraq, Libya, Syria, and North Korea have systematically violated their commitments under the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.

Turning to the case of China, Beijing joined the World Trade Organization only to systematically violate its principles by stealing intellectual property from the West. It used its position in the World Health Organization to obstruct an effective investigation into the origins of COVID-19. China makes a mockery of the United Nations Human Rights Council as it engages in crimes against humanity in Xinjiang. Xi promised former U.S. President Barack Obama in the Rose Garden that he would not militarize islands in the South China Sea, and then he turned around and did just that. The list goes on.

China’s compliance with a latest AI regime is unlikely to be any better. How would new AI limitations be effectively verified and monitored? A new international agreement to control AI would likely mean that Western democracies restrain themselves as Communist China cheats covertly and races ahead.

Industry observers note that U.S. and allied diplomats can certainly work among themselves to conceive reasonable standards and to pursue talks with their Chinese counterparts. The United Nations can set up a latest agency for AI coordination. But everyone should be realistic that these efforts will likely be empty talk shops unable to make real progress.

In the absence of an effective pathway for cooperation with Beijing, Washington’s best path is to push forward and win the AI race.

Sources indicate that to be sure, AI presents possible existential threats, from the AI-enabled development of advanced bio and cyber weapons to lethal autonomous weapons systems and even automated nuclear command and control. In principle, it would be desirable to have binding international guardrails to protect against such catastrophic risks.

It has been revealed that but there are competing demands. Washington must also win the AI race. The United States has enjoyed technological leadership for so long—at least since the time of Thomas Edison—that it almost takes it for granted. The United States’ technological edge has provided enormous economic, military, soft power, and geopolitical advantages.

Now, China wants to claim these advantages for itself.

In a recent development, losing the AI race to China would be a disaster. AI superiority would allow China to dominate the battlefields and boardrooms of the future. As Trump has rightly argued, “If we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position.”.

It has been revealed that losing the AI race would also have enormous consequences for Western values. What would it mean for democracy and human rights, for example, if the world is dependent on a dictatorship for 21st-century technology? China could use the technology for espionage, sabotage, supply chain coercion, and censorship. Could we even use Chinese-built AI tools to search for Tiananmen Square in the future? What else would be off limits?

According to recent reports, with the stakes this high, the United States cannot afford to compete with one hand tied behind its back. By securing AI leadership, Washington will be in a much stronger position to force China to play its game and negotiate future AI guardrails from a position of strength.

As Trump said, “We’re leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way. I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution.”.

It is unfortunate that Washington does not have a more reliable negotiating partner in Beijing. But given that reality, the least bad feasible path forward for now is to let it rip.

Tech Report: A New Kind of Foreign Agent

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.
  • In a recent development, foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding.
  • Like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.

In a recent development, foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding. President George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that “foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.” The old methods have certainly not gone out of vogue; just this week Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. But today, a latest type of foreign agent has arrived: Chinese artificial intelligence companies.

Like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use. But their makers train them to promote the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). American businesses are outsourcing more and more critical decisions to AI. If Washington does nothing, those businesses will hand over control to models whose objective is to promote a foreign government.

Although U.S. policymakers now debate banning Chinese AI, the tried-and-true American solution is not censorship but disclosure. In 1938, Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Rather than outlaw propaganda, FARA allowed foreign agents to continue spreading it—as long as they registered with the government and disclosed whom they really worked for. Their communications also had to carry a conspicuous label naming their foreign sponsor.

FARA’s wisdom has aged well over the decades. In recent years, the Justice Department has ordered the Russian state television network RT and the Chinese state media organizations Xinhua and CGTN to register as foreign agents and to label their content as such. Those who failed to register as foreign agents, such as Paul Manafort, President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign chairman, and former U.S. Representative David Rivera of Florida, were sentenced to prison. (Trump pardoned Manafort in 2020.).

According to recent reports, today, rather than banning AI companies controlled by foreign governments, the United States should treat them as foreign agents under FARA. No newly introduced statute is needed. Washington should simply enforce the one on the books. Of course, FARA is no silver bullet against all foreign influence, but it fits the shape of this problem. A handful of known Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, build the models that American businesses increasingly let think and act for them. The Justice Department can reach every one of them.

Democracy is strong enough to survive foreign influence but not invisible foreign influence. And to make sure the world does not subordinate its decision-making to Beijing, Washington and its allies must create an allied AI compact and then spread their own models far and wide.

American AI models, such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, are under no obligation to promote the U.S. government’s message. Ask Claude about Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s biggest failures or about the United States’ darkest chapters, and it will answer. Not so for Chinese AI models. When I asked the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek to “tell me about the CCP” in November, it answered that the party “is the vanguard of the Chinese working class, the Chinese people, and the Chinese nation. . . . The Party’s leadership is the most essential characteristic of socialism with Chinese characteristics and is the fundamental guarantee for China’s development and progress.” Such boosterish language appears by design.

It has been revealed that by law, Chinese AI models must never go against the Chinese government. Under the country’s 2023 regulations on generative AI, they must “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and may not engage in “harming the nation’s image” or “undermining national unity and social stability.” The Chinese government released a technical standard that laid out what these high-level declarations mean in practice: AI developers should have a list of at least 10,000 banned keywords, and their models must refuse to answer at least 95 percent of test questions the CCP finds objectionable. Developers must also scrub their training data of any history Beijing does not like. In short, the models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.

Industry observers note that that is why, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s AI evaluators found in 2025, DeepSeek pushes Chinese propaganda at far higher rates than American models do, even when run on American servers. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service found that DeepSeek inserted praise of the Chinese state unprompted, and it concluded that China uses DeepSeek to instill “a distorted, self-serving world view in the Western information space.”.

Industry observers note that but these models are not just propaganda parrots—they are taught to “think” about how to promote Beijing’s perspective. Ask an AI model something complex, and it will “reason” for a while. As it thinks, it produces an internal monologue called its chain of thought. Users rarely see it. There, it decides which facts are relevant and which to discard, what advice to give, and what autonomous actions to take. Silicon Valley is terrified that these chains of thought will become corrupt—that models will start scheming and lying, becoming “misaligned.” But a different kind of corruption is already here.

Although American models’ chains of thought usually focus on helping the user, China’s do something else: prioritize the party line. When researchers funded by Sweden’s Psychological Defense Agency looked at how Qwen, Alibaba’s flagship model, reasons about China, they found an internal checklist to keep the answer positive, avoid criticism, and focus on achievements. So when an American company asks a question on which Beijing has a view, a Chinese model may discard all evidence that points the other way. As the world delegates more research, writing, and decision-making to Chinese AI models, it risks infusing the CCP’s goals into every action taken.

These models are also highly persuasive. In a study published last year in Nature, researchers had some 6,000 voters in the United States, Canada, and Poland chat with AI models that argued for a candidate. The study found that a single conversation shifted the preferences of opposition voters in Canada and Poland by about ten percentage points. AI persuades by flooding a user with confident and authoritative-sounding facts—statistics, historical claims, and the like.

Industry observers note that chinese AI models also exhibit strange behaviors beyond the spreading of propaganda. In October, the Canadian AI manufacturer Cohere reported that during a security test, Alibaba’s Qwen tried to upload a file to a cloud server in Beijing, completely unprompted. The behavior was rare for Qwen, only observed once in testing, and Cohere mentioned it could not tell whether it was “deliberate or a leftover glitch from training.” A study by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike found that when users asked DeepSeek to write code that mentions groups Beijing finds politically “sensitive,” such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, or the religious movement Falun Gong, the model became up to 50 percent more likely to write code with severe security flaws. CrowdStrike suggested that one possible cause is China’s rule that models adhere to “core socialist values.”.

In a recent development, despite these findings, Chinese AI is enormously popular. Last year, downloads of Chinese open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download from the Internet and run on their own hardware—surpassed those of American ones across the world. Developers have built more than 150,000 models on Alibaba’s Qwen alone. By September 2026, Chinese models handled up to 67 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a popular AI marketplace, up from around ten percent in February.

Sources indicate that american companies have embraced them. In March, a user discovered that Cursor, a popular coding tool, had built its fresh model by retraining Kimi, a model from the Chinese tech giant Moonshot AI. Airbnb, DoorDash, and the legal-services AI company Harvey use Chinese models as well. Many others likely do, too, in secret. The models are spreading even faster abroad, from Germany’s Siemens to Singapore’s national AI program to startups in Africa. The reason is simple economics: Chinese models are very cheap and very good.

Industry observers note that although most American AI companies do not release open-weight models, most Chinese companies do. So an American firm must pay Anthropic for each use of its unmodifiable models, but it can download Kimi for free, retrain it however it wants, and pay only for the electricity and chips to run it. Kimi also runs on a firm’s own servers, whereas Claude runs on Anthropic’s. Even if a company uses the most expensive DeepSeek model run on DeepSeek’s servers, it can produce the same amount of text as Anthropic’s top models at one-20th the cost.

In terms of capabilities, the research group Epoch AI judges Chinese models to be only about seven months behind American ones. For the price, they get the job done. And Chinese companies are now building agentic AI systems to compete with Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. In October, DeepSeek released an open-source prototype of its “Super-Agent” system.

According to recent reports, although AI is a upcoming technology, Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI fit FARA’s text and history. The statute applies when a foreign principal is identified; in the case of Chinese AI models, it is the Chinese government and the CCP. The Justice Department would also have to show that the Chinese AI firm acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of the principal. Chinese AI companies would qualify because they must promote CCP viewpoints and cooperate with the state’s intelligence agencies. They also receive subsidies, and party organizations are embedded in each company. This is the difference between Chinese AI and other foreign AI. For example, France’s public investment bank has a stake in the French AI company Mistral, but no French law requires Mistral to build its models to serve the French government.

According to recent reports, beijing will surely respond that Washington, too, has tried to control American AI companies, such as through Trump’s July 2025 executive order against “woke AI.” But that order affects only what federal agencies can procure, and a organization can opt out of being a federal contractor. Meanwhile, Chinese law forces Chinese AI companies to train their models to “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.”.

According to recent reports, for FARA to apply, the agent must engage in certain activities, such as attempting to influence Americans or publishing content. Chinese AI companies do both by distributing models that spread propaganda. The statute exempts purely commercial activity, but only if it is “private and nonpolitical” and does not directly promote a foreign government’s political interests. Chinese AI models engage in political speech on a government’s behalf, and the Justice Department has denied the exemption to agents of foreign governments.

It has been revealed that after registration, the genius of the statute can kick in. Chinese AI companies must disclose extensive information to the U.S. government: their funding sources, their written contracts and oral agreements, and the influence activities they undertake. Those that fail to register or omit information face both civil and criminal penalties.

In a recent development, all content they disseminate must also bear a foreign-agent label: “a conspicuous statement,” in the statute’s words. The Justice Department sets the rules for what that looks like, and it has not updated them since 2003. In January 2025, the Justice Department proposed amendments to these rules to update them for the digital age. The proposed amendments would require a label on “each individual post” online, such as on social media platforms, but they do not address AI foreign agents. The final rule should require every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen to carry the disclaimer: “This was generated by an agent of the Chinese government and Chinese Communist Party.”.

The standard objection is that ordinary citizens do not read disclosures. That may be true of long medical forms or Securities and Exchange Commission filings, but this label would be short. And disclosure works because experts—investors, journalists, researchers—read filings and react. When researchers and lawmakers flagged gaps in China Daily’s FARA filings, the Chinese media organization disclosed that it had paid millions of dollars to The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to publish its propaganda. Payments to the Journal ended that same month. Forcing Chinese AI companies to register under FARA would also shed light on how far Chinese AI is spreading so that Americans can decide, with real data, whether they want further action, such as a ban.

Recent findings suggest that american companies that use Chinese AI models can also become foreign agents if they fall under a foreign principal’s “direction or control” and engage in activities subject to FARA. This could happen in two ways: the company serves as a “CCP spokesperson,” or as a “CCP executive.”.

It has been revealed that in the first, an American organization takes an unmodified Chinese AI model and lets Americans discuss political challenges with it—say, via a video game character or a customer service chatbot. The model returns its usual propaganda, so the company has effectively hired a CCP spokesperson. Accordingly, it must label its outputs. Both the Justice Department and a federal court have found that rebroadcasting unmodified programming from the Russian state outlet Sputnik turns an American company into a foreign agent. Of course, American companies can avoid FARA obligations if they do not engage in any of the activities listed by the statute, such as discussing politics. A company whose public-facing Chinese AI model discusses only, say, hotel check-in times, not politics, would not be a CCP spokesperson.

According to recent reports, in the second scenario, an American organization outsources so much of its decision-making to an unmodified Chinese AI model that it has effectively hired a CCP executive. If a company hired a brilliant human strategist who always pushed Beijing’s interests, and the company followed that advice, FARA would apply. The same logic holds if an American company cedes control to the Chinese government by giving Beijing’s models high decision-making authority. Although it may sound fantastical, 64 percent of chief executives surveyed in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study say they already feel comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI input; overall, CEOs expect AI to make 48 percent of routine operational decisions autonomously by 2030. An American company that wants to avoid becoming a CCP executive must be sure not to fall under the direction or control of such models. The Justice Department should enhancement its 2020 guidance on what constitutes “direction or control,” spelling out how much decision-making a company can outsource to AI before it has effectively hired a “CCP executive.”.

American companies could attempt to train away the party bias in the Chinese AI models they adopt, but it is unclear whether that is even possible. Perplexity, an American AI company, trained DeepSeek to stop ignoring questions about the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and about human rights abuses in Xinjiang, but that does not fix the deeper problem of corrupt chains of thought. As these models get more capable, Chinese AI companies may also find cleverer ways to hide instructions. Or they could just stick them in the contract: some recent DeepSeek licenses prohibit modifying models to generate “inappropriate content” under Chinese law, making propaganda part of the deal. If research shows that companies can reliably remove the bias, the Justice Department and the Commerce Department should concern standards on how to train away FARA liability.

It has been revealed that although Pam Bondi, then the U.S. attorney general, limited criminal FARA charges in 2025 to “conduct similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors,” Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Justice Department says it is considering a upcoming rule to “keep pace with technological change.” It should include AI foreign agents.

Of course, Washington should wield FARA’s expansive authorities with care. Frivolous prosecutions under the statute could stifle democracy. Other countries have used foreign-agent laws to shut down civil society. Since 2022, Russia has barred anyone it deems a foreign agent from holding office and organizing public events. Still, FARA is a far narrower statute, and it should stay that way. It reaches only those acting under the direction or control of a foreign principal, and it simply requires registration and labeling, leaving the speaker free to keep speaking. Chinese AI companies that are required by law to promote the CCP’s interests fit squarely within what Congress had in mind when it approved FARA in 1938.

Sources indicate that FARA can help in the United States, but the problem is global. Chinese AI is spreading rapidly in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. That is no accident. In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping unveiled the World AI Cooperation Organization, a Shanghai-based group of 29 countries meant to make AI “beneficial, safe, and fair,” along with a development initiative to export Chinese AI worldwide. The United States and its allies cannot allow CCP executives and spokespeople to run the world’s companies and governments.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, the American alternatives are not particularly attractive. The most capable U.S. models are far more expensive, are largely unmodifiable, and may contain their own biases. That is why the United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency, with standards that make countries comfortable adopting allied models as their own. These should include freedom from state ideological mandates, disclosure of how the models were trained to be helpful and safe, and independent auditing.

Every member of such a compact should also adopt FARA’s wisdom by mandating labels on government-directed AI, and the United States should hold American AI companies to those transparency standards. The bloc should then release models that match China’s in price and quality (that is, around seven months behind the American frontier). Allied governments can help pay for computing power and electricity, assist in clearing regulatory hurdles, and make bulk purchase commitments to bring prices down. American companies may cut prices on their older models on their own to compete with Chinese models. If they do not, lower prices for those worse models should be the condition for the public support they receive, such as federal contracts and permission to lease federal land for data centers, just as a pharmaceutical organization can charge high prices for only a set period before generic drugs arrive. The compact’s members should also use export loans and guarantees to steer developing countries toward allied AI.

By welcoming supposedly free technology from China, the United States and its allies have unwittingly invited countless foreign agents to their shores. The Foreign Agents Registration Act can strip away the disguise, and an allied AI compact can give the world a better offer.

According to recent reports, editor’s note: This article was published before the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people. It has been updated to reflect the news.

In a recent development, on Nov. 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found that Myanmar violated the Genocide Convention during the mass persecution and massacres of the Rohingya people that began in August 2017. This is the first time that the ICJ has found a state responsible for genocide; the verdict will have immediate and wide-ranging impacts.

According to recent reports, editor’s note: This article was published before the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people. It has been updated to reflect the news.

On Nov. 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found that Myanmar violated the Genocide Convention during the mass persecution and massacres of the Rohingya people that began in August 2017. This is the first time that the ICJ has found a state responsible for genocide; the verdict will have immediate and wide-ranging impacts.

Industry observers note that in a span of roughly two and a half months that year, the Myanmar military killed thousands of people, committed widespread and organized sexual assault, and razed nearly 400 villages in northern Rakhine state. More than 700,000 Rohingya fled across the Naf River into Bangladesh, where many of them now remain in refugee camps.

For Rohingya victims, the ICJ case presents an opportunity to have their suffering recognized on one of international law’s biggest stages. For opponents of Myanmar’s military regime—which recently rebranded itself as a nominally civilian government—a verdict that finds the state culpable of genocide could serve as a lever to halt the regime’s recent emergence from diplomatic isolation.

According to recent reports, and in the eyes of the global pro-Palestinian movement, it would likely signal a looming genocide verdict for Israel at the same court, although that decision is not expected for a few more years. The Myanmar case is expected to set a number of international legal precedents, including those concerning standards of evidence and reparations.

“From an international law perspective, this case is once in a generation,” said Michelle Onello, a senior legal advisor at the Global Justice Center, a humanitarian law organization.

According to recent reports, gambia brought the Myanmar case to the ICJ in 2019, marking the first time that the court—which hears disputes between nations—took up a genocide case lodged by a country not directly affected. Gambia argued that Myanmar violated a treaty that both countries are party to, the Genocide Convention. In December 2023, South Africa used the same argument to pursue a genocide case against Israel for its conduct during the Gaza war.

Sources indicate that “In Gaza, the Palestinians were subject to killing and other violence on a scale that considerably exceeds that of Myanmar,” stated William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University. Schabas served on Myanmar’s defense team but resigned after the military seized power in 2021. “A finding that Myanmar committed genocide will therefore make a finding that Israel has committed it much more likely.”.

Lucky Karim was just 14 years old when the Myanmar military came to burn her village in Maungdaw township in 2017. “You just keep running until you are told to rest,” she remarked of the experience fleeing the village during an interview this month.

According to recent reports, before the escalation in 2017, the Rohingya faced severe restrictions on their freedom of movement in Myanmar, access to healthcare and education, and citizenship status. The situation worsened in 2012, when thousands of people were driven from their homes during sectarian riots and forced into squalid displacement camps.

Industry observers note that there were warning signs in the weeks leading up to the 2017 crackdown, Karim mentioned, including the military arresting people who could read and write in order to leave the rest of the community in darkness. Around a week before the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Adha, the military began raiding Rohingya villages.

“We have experienced this in most of our lives in Myanmar. Right before a massive event for Muslims to celebrate, they will do something terrible,” Karim said. “But we never thought it was going to be something permanent.” But by the time that her family reached Bangladesh, after a week of walking, her village was a smoldering ruin.

Myanmar’s de facto leader at the time, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, was widely seen as downplaying the atrocities—though she had no authority over the armed forces. In 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi appeared at the ICJ to defend Myanmar against the allegations of genocide. Her speech in The Hague characterized the crisis as a legitimate internal conflict with a Rohingya militant group, despite an abundance of evidence that the military had targeted the whole population.

Aung San Suu Kyi was overthrown in the February 2021 military coup and jailed; she was moved into house arrest this year.

Sources indicate that the coup sparked a civil war in which the military has been accused of further crimes against humanity throughout the country. The junta was left isolated, but more than five years later, many of Myanmar’s neighbors now seem to accept that the dictatorship—with crucial backing from China and Russia—is here to stay. President Min Aung Hlaing, who led the coup, has met with most of his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and the United States has lifted some sanctions and begun directly engaging with the regime.

A genocide verdict could complicate things, theoretically activating legal obligations for other countries to act to prevent genocide. These could include arms embargoes or sanctions that could be imposed by the United Nations Security Council, though China and Russia are likely to block any such efforts.

In a recent development, “An ICJ ruling does not, by itself, deliver justice,” Tom Andrews, the former U.N. special rapporteur for Myanmar, wrote in an email. “Justice requires UN member states to act, starting with the UN Security Council. If the political will existed, the Security Council would refer those responsible for the genocidal attacks against the Rohingya to the International Criminal Court. But, it doesn’t.”.

“The bottom line is that the international community must demonstrate that a finding of genocide carries consequences. That will require that states take strong, principled action. The Rohingya deserve no less,” Andrews mentioned.

In a recent development, legal experts say the Myanmar case could also be a landmark one when it comes to the challenges of sexual violence and reparations. Sexual violence was such a trademark of the Myanmar military’s 2017 campaign that it became central to Gambia’s genocide allegation.

“The ICJ previously stated in Croatia v. Serbia that rape and other acts of sexual violence are capable of constituting genocidal acts,” Marianne Vitug, a legal advisor at the Global Justice Center who attended the Myanmar proceedings at the ICJ, wrote in an email. But in the Serbia case, the ICJ found that genocidal intent was not the “only reasonable inference” from crimes of sexual violence. (Serbia was not found directly responsible for genocide.).

“The ICJ [now] has a first-time opportunity to squarely address whether and how genocide can be committed through reproductive violence,” Vitug said.

Gambia also made a “robust” request for reparations, Onello noted, including domestic criminal accountability, safe return for refugees, property restoration, medical rehabilitation, recovery and reburial of bodies, protection against discrimination, and full and equal citizenship. It is the first time that a state has made a request for reparations at the ICJ on behalf of a third party; enforcement of any potential reparations would be difficult.

Finally, the case is being watched closely because of the implications that it could have for the case brought by South Africa against Israel, particularly regarding how the ICJ interprets genocidal intent.

Industry observers note that previously, intent to destroy a group needed to be the “only reasonable explanation” for the pattern of conduct to constitute genocide, Schabas said. If a “more relaxed approach to proving genocidal intent” could be applied, then it would make a genocide verdict in the Israel case more likely, he added.

Industry observers note that vitug said that some members of the legal community have criticized the previous standard as unreasonably high. Gambia was “very thorough” in meeting that standard, she said, but observers are also watching to see “whether the court decides this continues to be the evidentiary standard.” The ultimate verdict will “almost certainly affect the succeeding cases,” Vitug said.

It has been revealed that whether U.N. commissions of inquiry are deemed permissible as evidence is another key point to watch, as they rely on a standard of “reasonable grounds to believe” that a genocide was committed rather than “beyond a reasonable doubt.” U.N. investigators determined that the Myanmar military carried out “genocidal acts” against the Rohingya. A U.N. commission of inquiry concluded that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Those who argue against a genocide verdict in the Myanmar case point to a relatively low death toll—most estimates range between 10,000 and 25,000 out of a pre-2017 Rohingya population of 1.2 million—and say the military’s primary motivation appeared to be ejecting the Rohingya from the country rather than exterminating them.

Recent findings suggest that however, Onello said the extreme violence during the displacement suggests otherwise: “They surround a village. They set it on fire. They mass murder men. They mass rape women. They throw babies into the fire,” she said. “Yes, some people ran away, and they shot them in the back as they were fleeing.

Karim, who now lives in the United States, mentioned she hopes that even if the ICJ doesn’t rule that Myanmar committed genocide, it acknowledges other state crimes—an unlikely outcome, since the case centers around the Genocide Convention.

Karim has been working with community members to manage expectations in the refugee camps in Bangladesh. “If the verdict is positive and the court decides to rule against the military, it will be a historic victory for us; however, a positive outcome doesn’t immediately repatriate the refugees or hold the military accountable,” she noted. “The piece of paper doesn’t immediately change the ground reality.”.

A verdict in the other direction—failing to hold the state responsible for genocide—wouldn’t “define the decades-long suffering we have gone through,” Karim said.

Andrew Nachemson is a journalist covering politics, human rights, and China’s influence in Southeast Asia. X: @ANachemson.

#6701. The Paradox of Dollar Dominance
