📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Congressional watchdog leaders Randall Schriver and Mike Kuiken warn China could exploit American chips and AI to strengthen its military.

A new congressional report is urging the U.S. to restrict investments in China’s aerospace sector and withhold taxpayer funding from companies that build military capabilities for U.S. adversaries, warning that Western commercial partnerships transferred technology and expertise to Chinese firms with military ties.

The 65-page report, titled "China's Wingmen: How Western Government Policy Enabled China's Rise in the Skies," follows a year-long investigation by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, led by Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Ranking Member Ro Khanna, D-Calif. It examined how legal commercial partnerships transferred advanced technology and manufacturing expertise to Chinese military-linked companies.

China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) is the country's military, which the committee notes has benefited from civilian aerospace technology transfers.

In a recent development, "American and European companies transferred technology to China that could be used against our brave men and women in uniform. With the CCP’s military-civil fusion there are no private companies in China," Moolenaar remarked in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN.

China's domestically produced C919 passenger jet sits on display at the Singapore Airshow on Feb. 4, 2026, in Singapore. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images).

"The PLA will exploit civilian technology and use it to advance its military ambitions and that is what happened here.".

The report singled out European aerospace giant Airbus, which receives U.S. defense contracts while maintaining manufacturing partnerships in China. Although Airbus sold its stake in an AVIC affiliate in 2025, its commercial partnerships with the Chinese aerospace conglomerate continue, according to the committee.

The bipartisan panel examined at least six U.S.-China joint ventures involving American defense suppliers GE Aerospace, Honeywell Aerospace and RTX subsidiary Collins Aerospace.

Industry observers note that investigators found that GE transferred foundational avionics technology to a joint venture with a subsidiary of AVIC, the Chinese state-owned conglomerate that develops military aircraft, including the J-20 stealth fighter. The committee noted GE withheld its original joint venture agreement despite repeated requests.

RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER.

An Airbus aircraft assembly facility in Tianjin, China, on Oct. 25, 2025. The European aerospace manufacturer opened its second A320-family final assembly line in the city that month. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images).

It has been revealed that the American companies maintained that their Chinese partnerships supported civilian aircraft and complied with U.S. export controls. The report also cited previous export-control settlements involving all three companies but did not establish that the partnerships under investigation violated U.S. law.

In a recent development, "We appreciate the Committee’s work ensuring the U.S. retains its position as the world’s commercial aviation leader while protecting our most sensitive technologies. We have and will continue to follow relevant U.S. laws and regulations, as the report acknowledges,"a Collins Aerospace spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

Sources indicate that "GE Aerospace takes national security, compliance, and the protection of its intellectual property seriously, and we work closely with the U.S. government – including this Committee – to ensure we continue to do so," a GE Aerospace spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

GE also stated its joint venture with AVIC involves older avionics technology sold exclusively in China, not jet engines, and that the arrangement includes safeguards intended to protect sensitive information and ensure compliance with U.S. law.

AMERICA'S ENEMIES PREPARE TO TAKE THE NEXT MAJOR WAR INTO OUTER SPACE.

According to recent reports, A J-20 stealth fighter jet of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force performs at the China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, or Airshow China, in Zhuhai, Guangdong province, China Nov. 9, 2022. (China Daily via Reuters).

Honeywell Aerospace told Fox News Digital that its commercial partnerships were fully licensed and approved by the U.S. government, adding that it cooperated transparently with the committee and continues to comply with U.S. export laws.

The committee urged the Federal Aviation Administration not to certify Chinese-manufactured aircraft, citing state subsidies and Beijing's refusal to release a final report on the 2022 China Eastern Airlines crash.

"The report’s only recommendation directed at the FAA is that they do not certify Chinese-made aircraft, which the agency has not done," an FAA spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

#6681. Breaking: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

Breaking: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
  • At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
  • Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

Industry observers note that yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

According to recent reports, in recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

In a recent development, at the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

The success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

International efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

Industry observers note that in the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

It has been revealed that today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

Sources indicate that worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

Industry observers note that there is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

Recent findings suggest that A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France announced the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

Recent findings suggest that simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

Recent findings suggest that the integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

Together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will rapidly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

Sources indicate that political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

In this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

But these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

Wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

War also creates new dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

Sources indicate that finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to new waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

The world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

According to recent reports, but it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

Recent findings suggest that spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

It has been revealed that from day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

Deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

In a recent development, countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

Sources indicate that investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

Yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

Reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

Sources indicate that some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

Other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

Recent findings suggest that the twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

Industry observers note that all of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

Strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

The first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An update to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly notable, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The new seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats right now occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

Permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

According to recent reports, A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

In a recent development, another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral Latest START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

Recent findings suggest that yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

Technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

According to recent reports, the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

Proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a newly introduced UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

Halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

In a recent development, ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

Industry observers note that international financial institutions must be able to deliver financing quickly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

This is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, debuted with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

According to recent reports, A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

In a recent development, chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a big hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit kicked off in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Wednesday with a two-hour meeting between Xi and Putin. During the talks, Xi highlighted the importance of the China-Russia relationship and touted the necessity of a multipolar world.

Recent findings suggest that in a keynote address later that day, he further vowed to defy trade protectionism and maintain a “free and open” system, painting Beijing as a stable economic partner that can counter the White House’s volatile tariff war. Putin echoed that message in his own speech while criticizing Western sanctions imposed on Russia due to its war against Ukraine.

The meetings and speeches did not signal a dramatic shift in policy; Xi has already used this week’s Asia-Pacific summitry to curry favor with some of the region’s most influential allies, from Canada to Peru. However, the timing was notable, as just a few hours after the Xi-Putin talks, Xi was on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to personally greet Trump with a warm embrace.

According to recent reports, such a personal welcome is uncommon for the Chinese president, who usually sends a high-level representative to meet with foreign leaders when they touch down in China. However, the friendly greeting may be an effort to parallel Trump’s own approach to their relationship, as Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs to his jet when the latter flew to Washington in September.

Recent findings suggest that wednesday’s red-carpet welcome for the U.S. president also included an honor guard, a military flyover, an array of flowers, and a cheering crowd. Trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Mike Kuiken, the vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar ahead of Trump’s Asia trip. “[T]his is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy,” Kuiken added.

Xi later hosted Putin, Trump, and the other gathered dignitaries at an APEC welcome banquet, during which the Chinese leader outlined the primary goals of the summit. “We will discuss steps to expand mutual openness, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, extend opportunities for result-oriented cooperation across various fields, and strive to deliver more tangible results on the ground,” Xi remarked.

As for what will be on the agenda for Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Trump has stressed his interest in discussing the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars as well as nuclear disarmament; however, experts expect Xi to try to steer the conversation away from nuclear arms collaboration.

Sources indicate that putin, meanwhile, appears optimistic about Thursday’s dialogue, insisting that the talks will likely have a significant impact on global affairs. “I therefore expect significant potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting,” Putin said.

Widening strikes. Iranian forces targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait on Wednesday for the first time since September, upending a roughly two-month pause on strikes against U.S. military sites. That same day, Tehran also released several attacks on Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. Both small Persian Gulf countries claimed to have intercepted Iran’s aerial assaults.

In a recent development, wednesday’s strikes marked the latest round of tit-for-tat attacks between Iran and the United States. According to Iran’s military, the operation against Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base on Wednesday was in retaliation for a U.S. airstrike on Iran’s Qeshm Island the day before. Qeshm serves as a staging ground for Iranian forces targeting global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and it hosts an expansive underground tunnel network that is often used as a base of operations for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

In a recent development, “If ​the enemy repeats its mistake,” Iranian Army chief Amir Hatami noted in a video posted by state media on Wednesday, “we have the readiness and the prepares to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations.” Such a threat comes one day after seven U.S. officials told CNN that Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. The White House has stressed that there is no imminent threat to the U.S. homeland.

Strapped for cash. The European Commission proposed a newly introduced $49.5 billion loan to Ukraine on Wednesday to help Kyiv avert its looming cash crisis and bolster its defenses against Russia. “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated. “And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”.

Sources indicate that last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined a $76.8 billion funding gap for 2027, at a time when Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure. Notably, Moscow is expected to double its drone deployments next year to 20 million units, which EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said will likely force Kyiv to allocate some 62 percent of its military budget on drones.

A nearly $50 billion EU loan will cover roughly two-thirds of this gap; aid will be split between weapons funding and civilian needs, such as for hospitals and schools, and foreign allies will be encouraged to supply the rest. Von der Leyen expressed confidence on Wednesday that all 27 EU member states will support the loan. However, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia have already noted that they will not take part in the latest funding round, prompting Germany to threaten to veto the bloc’s seven-year budget until all nations are on board.

In a recent development, AI cheating concerns. Around 550,000 South Korean students are preparing to take their university entrance exam, known as the Suneung, at more than 1,300 testing centers across the country on Thursday. The high-stress event is known for causing minor disruptions to businesses, as traffic is redirected, offices and tourist attractions open later, and extra trains run to accommodate test-taking.

However, this year’s exam will also include new restrictions to crack down on potential cheating after the top scorer of another professional test admitted on Sunday to using artificial intelligence to secure his suspiciously high score; the individual only got one question wrong on the tax accountant exam by using a miniature camera, a phone, and AI.

Industry observers note that the admission prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to convene an emergency cabinet meeting this week to discuss what the prime minister described as the “social evil” of AI-empowered fraud. “Cheating on exams using advanced equipment is no different from stealing the scores of hundreds of thousands of examinees who worked hard,” Lee wrote on X on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that among the newly introduced testing measures, all smartphones will be confiscated, glasses and watches will be inspected, and some public Wi-Fi spots will be blocked. A reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) will also be given to anyone who reports an instance of cheating involving advanced equipment.

Recent findings suggest that A packed week of high-stakes summitry has kept Trump busy and, perhaps, hungry. But Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. believes that he has the perfect solution. The host of this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations conference arranged for the U.S. president to receive a late-night delivery of Jollibee fried chicken on Wednesday as a sort of pick-me-up after a hard day’s work. Jollibee is the Philippines’s most popular fast-food chain and represents what Marcos described as a “taste of Manila.”.

FP’s World Brief writer would like to note that she too has been kept busy and famished by this week’s onslaught of news and would also enjoy some Jollibee fried chicken if Marcos wants to put in a second order.

Congo’s Escalating Ebola Crisis

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • The highlights this week: Health leaders issue upcoming warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.
  • It has been revealed that six months into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, the rare Bundibugyo variant of the virus demonstrates no sign of slowing down in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders glitch fresh warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders issue upcoming warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

It has been revealed that six months into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, the rare Bundibugyo variant of the virus demonstrates no sign of slowing down in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is exacerbated by an underfunded health system and armed conflict in eastern provinces, where global mining projects have led to increased disease transmission.

The outbreak is “still serious, and is still not under control,” noted Jean Kaseya, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC. The death toll since the outbreak began in May has passed 5,500 people, with more than 11,000 people infected, according to Congolese government figures released last week.

Infections are now spreading at double the rate as when the outbreak began, according to Kaseya. More than 80 percent of newly introduced cases are emerging outside of known contact lists, and more than 65 percent of deaths have occurred outside of healthcare facilities, he added.

Kaseya called the lack of coordination between Congo’s government and foreign donors “a collective failure,” urging donors to release $1.6 billion in pledged aid.

Industry observers note that international donors have disbursed more than $962 million to organizations that are implementing Congo’s Ebola response. But around $700 million of that sum was unaccounted for as of last month, according to Kaseya. The Africa CDC mentioned that it was too early to attribute this discrepancy to embezzlement, but an investigation is underway.

In 2020, Congo’s former health minister was convicted of embezzling more than $400,000 from funds intended to fight Ebola during the 2018-2020 outbreak.

Meanwhile, Congolese health workers—who have not been paid for months—have gone on strike. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warned last week that ambulances had run out of fuel, staff were untrained, and that the Congolese government and United Nations agencies needed to “strengthen oversight and accountability.” MSF has called the outbreak “out of control.”.

In a recent development, for Congo, dealing with the Ebola crisis requires tackling systemic problems beyond healthcare, including poverty, conflict, and inefficient governance. But Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi appears to be focused on cementing his grip on power. On Nov. 9, he signed a law that critics say could grant him a third term in office.

It has been revealed that congo’s 2006 constitution allows a maximum of two presidential terms and explicitly prevents parliament from changing those rules under any circumstance. The new law lowers the threshold for holding national referendums and permits constitutional overhauls through referendums “in case of absolute necessity.”.

It has been revealed that tshisekedi became president in January 2019; his second term ends in 2028. He has said that he is not seeking a third term but would serve one if given a mandate by voters. “I have not asked for a third term, but I tell you this: If the people want me to have a third term, I will accept,” Tshisekedi said in May.

On Nov. 1, the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, a newly introduced rebel alliance led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, sent a letter to U.S. officials and the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Congo warning that any constitutional changes could derail peace negotiations. Kabila’s alliance includes the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23.

The Trump administration negotiated a peace accord between Congo and Rwanda in December 2025 that seemed to prioritize securing U.S. access to Congo’s critical minerals over tackling domestic government reforms and bolstering a weak state. Expanded mining in Congo’s forests has increased human contact with animals that carry the Ebola virus, according to scientists.

Nearly one year on, amid an Ebola outbreak and on the precipice of further conflict, Congo is paying the price for the institutional neglect enshrined in the deal.

According to recent reports, wednesday, Nov. 18: An Egyptian court hears the retrial of Lina Attalah, the editor in chief of Mada Masr, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The U.N. has described the charges against Attalah as an assault on press freedom.

The U.N. Security Council hears a briefing from the International Criminal Court on its work in Libya.

In a recent development, thursday, Nov. 19, to Saturday, Dec. 19: Dak’Art, the biennale of contemporary African art, returns to Dakar, Senegal.

Wednesday, Nov. 25: The U.N. Security Council is due to renew its sanctions targeting al-Shabaab and other armed groups in Somalia.

Sources indicate that amnesty report on South Sudan. A upcoming report from Amnesty International accuses South Sudan’s government and U.N. peacekeepers of failing to act on advance warnings of a March massacre that killed more than 200 people. The report came ahead of an announcement that South Sudan would again delay general elections to February 2027.

The elections were previously scheduled for Dec. 22. The South Sudanese government did not cite a reason for the move, but authorities have repeatedly pushed back elections since 2022 amid a power struggle between President Salva Kiir and his ousted former deputy, Riek Machar.

A 2018 power-sharing arrangement between Kiir and Machar  broke down last year after an attack on a military base in Upper Nile state by an armed group known as the White Army, which killed more than 250 soldiers. Kiir accused Machar and his party’s military wing of colluding with the White Army, which Machar denied.

Machar is at the moment on trial for charges including treason.

Sources indicate that cape Verde elections. Cape Verdean President José Maria Neves was reelected on Sunday, capturing more than 63 percent of the vote amid record low turnout, according to provisional results. Neves’s main challenger, former Justice Minister Joana Rosa—the country’s first woman presidential candidate—conceded on Monday.

It has been revealed that the lack of opportunities for young people in Cape Verde was a major election topic. Rosa pledged to address issues facing young people, while Neves promised to organize a summit to address youth emigration. According to data released in July by Cape Verde’s statistics body, around 65 percent of people aged 15 to 35 said they intended to emigrate.

Neves’s party has dominated Cape Verdean politics since it gained independence from Portugal in 1975.

Madagascar’s ties to Russia. U.S. Africa Command’s deputy commander, John Brennan, warned against Madagascar’s strengthening ties with Russia last week, saying that Moscow is importing the “Sahel model” to the island.

In a recent development, “We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent,” Brennan stated in a media briefing. Since the country’s 2025 coup, Russia has supplied the military-backed government with weapons—amid repeated calls from young Madagascans for a return to democracy.

Recent findings suggest that some Africans perceived Brennan’s comments as lecturing from the United States. “America is not talking to Russia as a partner. It is talking to Madagascar as a client,” Fortune Madondo wrote in Modern Ghana, suggesting that the United States might condition assistance to needy Madagascar on its allegiance.

It has been revealed that the criticism underscored why it’s vital that U.S. officials consider how their comments land in Africa. If not framed carefully, they could play into Russia’s narrative that the United States is acting like a colonial power.

Ghana to boost local manufacturing. Ghana will invest $10 billion over four years in a domestically funded “upcoming economy” program to boost local manufacturing and jobs. Ghanaian Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson told parliament in his 2027 budget speech last Friday that the funds will increase refining capacity and reduce lower-value raw materials exports.

Recent findings suggest that around $1.5 billion of the package will be allocated to financing refining facilities for gold, manganese, bauxite, and lithium. The Ghanaian government stated it is relying on tax reforms already approved by parliament, better tax collection, and revenue from oil and minerals exports to finance the program.

The winner of this year’s 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza, has been cleared of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning short story, “The Blue Fighter,” after an October article in the Atlantic noted that the AI detection software Pangram found the story was entirely AI-generated.

According to recent reports, the Atlantic article sparked pushback from Africa’s literary community. Critics said AI detection tools are disproportionately weaponized against authors from marginalized backgrounds. Following a monthlong review, the Caine Prize’s board said that digital forensic evidence showed the article was human-written and that Kundizeza’s $13,000 award stands.

According to recent reports, nigeria’s surveillance state. An investigation by Ajibola Amzat for the Center for Collaborative Investigative Journalism found that Nigeria has spent billions of dollars of public funds on surveillance technology that is supposedly intended to fight insecurity—but is routinely used instead to monitor protesters, journalists, and government critics.

“Constitutionally guaranteed dissent is being watched and increasingly hunted while the terrorists and bandits freely operating in several corners of Nigeria’s 36 states remain elusive,” Amzat wrote.

It has been revealed that europe’s externalized borders. On Monday, five European countries—Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands—declared looks to send asylum-seekers who have exhausted all legal avenues to Rwanda.

In a recent development, in 2024, the United Kingdom scrapped a similar deal due to legal challenges over the country’s human rights record. Since 2019, the European Union has also funded a scheme operated by the U.N. refugee agency that temporarily evacuates refugees from Libya to Rwanda.

In light of this week’s news, we’re revisiting Sally Hayden’s 2020 Foreign Policy dispatch from Rwanda’s refugee centers. “At what point does the EU become responsible for refugees it has forced from its borders through externalization policies?” Hayden wrote at the time.

Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. X: @nosmotg.

#6675. Why Israel Is Losing America

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2397 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

Why Israel Is Losing America

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress.
  • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Vital Ally.
  • Sources indicate that american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Issues on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Vital Ally.

Sources indicate that american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

As I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

Things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a new paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

Sources indicate that this change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

Whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

It has been revealed that trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is currently marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he said himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

In a recent development, trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

It has been revealed that trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

It has been revealed that unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

Israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, revealed wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

Israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

Without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

According to recent reports, it is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

It has been revealed that israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s strategy for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

According to recent reports, israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

According to recent reports, israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of upcoming Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

Israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

According to recent reports, these steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

According to recent reports, if Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

Latest Update: What India Makes of Trump’s Asia Trip

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

Industry observers note that the highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan challenges a plea for medical treatment.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan issues a plea for medical treatment.

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday. Australia, India, Japan, and the United States announced initiatives including cybersecurity collaboration, a cable connectivity framework, and a maritime surveillance exercise.

The Quad meeting likely brought some relief for New Delhi. The grouping is crucial for India’s foreign-policy interests, bringing together some of its closest security partners in an effort to counter China. (However, the Quad states rarely mention Beijing in their public messaging about the grouping to avoid antagonizing the superpower.).

Though India has engineered a rapprochement with China in the last two years, taking steps to reduce border tensions and scale up trade and investment, they remain bitter strategic rivals. India prioritizes opportunities to work multilaterally to push back against China’s power through non-security collaborations in areas such as technology and infrastructure investment.

Scheduling problems and U.S.-India tensions have prevented high-level Quad engagement since September 2024. Quad supporters will point to Tuesday’s meeting as an indication of the grouping’s resilience, much like how it bounced back from quiescence in 2017—interestingly, with another summit in Manila when each member’s ties with China faced increasing strain.

Recent findings suggest that still, the Quad remains mired in uncertainty, mainly because of U.S. President Donald Trump. His administration’s signaling about taking a softer approach to competition with China, coupled with silence about the fate of the U.S. Indo-Pacific strategy, suggests that the current White House may not be prepared to throw its full support behind the Quad.

It has been revealed that though an incoming Democratic Congress might take a tougher line on China, this is unlikely to shape the Trump administration’s thinking on the Quad. As a result, the wider ASEAN summit arguably held more immediate significance for New Delhi than the Quad meeting.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has long sought to step up India’s game in Southeast Asia—a region home to key Indian partners and multiple growing economies. India has especially strong incentives to ramp up engagement given China’s large footprint there. In that sense, the stakes were high for Modi’s engagement with ASEAN leaders this week.

New Delhi will now closely watch as Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold a historic trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. There is a lack of clarity, but the discussion will reportedly include the Iran war and nuclear nonproliferation.

Industry observers note that such themes are unlikely to concern India, which has a strong interest in the wars in both Iran and Ukraine coming to an end. But the summit will be a vindication of sorts for New Delhi. In 2025, Trump slammed a meeting among Modi, Xi, and Putin in China; now, he is coming to the same table.

Recent findings suggest that however, the boost that China is likely to get from the trilateral isn’t ideal for India. The U.S., Chinese, and Russian leaders have never had such a formal face-to-face exchange. Beijing’s capacity to convene the three leaders, against a backdrop of long-standing U.S.-Russia hostility, is a major diplomatic achievement.

Sources indicate that for Upcoming Delhi, the biggest takeaway from this week’s high-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen is that the Quad leaders’ meeting was a relative sideshow. The ASEAN and APEC summits will generate more attention and hold more immediate significance for Indian policymakers.

In a recent development, bangladesh cleared for DFC investment. The U.S. International Development Finance Corp. (DFC) revealed on Monday that Bangladesh was now eligible to receive its financing. The DFC, which mobilizes private investment, has taken on added importance since the demise of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) last year.

Industry observers note that until now, Bangladesh was ineligible for DFC financing because of U.S. concerns about labor conditions in the country. Negotiations between Washington and Dhaka to address these concerns and clear the way go back to the Biden administration.

In a recent development, the announcement couldn’t come at a better time for Bangladesh, which faces serious development challenges and severe economic stress. Some of its most pressing challenges—such as fuel shortages and the world’s worst measles epidemic—are tied to energy and healthcare, two of DFC’s priority areas for investment.

DFC-funded projects could bring a boost to U.S.-Bangladesh relations. Development cooperation, for years embodied by the large USAID mission in Dhaka, has long been a major component of the relationship.

According to recent reports, khan challenges plea for medical treatment. Lawyers for Imran Khan sent an open letter on Monday from the jailed former prime minister to top judges in Pakistan, imploring them to secure better healthcare for Khan and his wife, who is also in prison. In the letter, Khan says he is suffering from high blood pressure and is at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

For months, Khan’s lawyers, family, and supporters have stated his health is worsening, while officials say he is stable and regularly monitored by prison doctors. In August, Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered Khan to be transferred to a private hospital for an extended period; he was instead brought to a government hospital and only briefly.

In a recent development, concern for Khan’s health was one reason why leaders of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party announced nationwide protests last month. But aside from some demonstrations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the only one governed by the PTI, the campaign didn’t materialize. The party might be back-channeling with the country’s leadership to secure concessions for Khan.

In a recent development, british royals visit India. The United Kingdom’s Prince William and Princess Catherine completed a three-day visit to India on Wednesday. They began their trip in Mumbai, where they participated in the Earthshot Prize ceremony. William founded the award, which focuses on developing new solutions to climate change.

The royal couple then traveled to Upcoming Delhi, where they met Modi. Their visit underscores the strong ties between India and its former colonizer. U.K.-India relations have deepened in recent years, buoyed most recently by a free trade deal that formally entered into force in July.

Sources indicate that for that matter, U.K.-Pakistan ties are also quite warm; William and Kate made a visit there in 2019. Deep people-to-people ties, thanks in part to large Indian and Pakistani diasporas in the U.K., help bolster these relationships. British colonial rule may have left a problematic legacy in the subcontinent, but diplomacy today is in a good place.

Recent findings suggest that new Delhi hosts an arts and culture forum this weekend under the banner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). The idea for the Civilisational Dialogue Forum came from India, which will head the event even though Pakistan is the current SCO chair. Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, will travel to New Delhi to represent Islamabad.

With India-Pakistan ties so tense in recent years, the rare occasions when senior ministers from one country have traveled to the other have mostly come in their capacity as SCO members.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari traveled to India for an SCO summit in 2023, while Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar went to Pakistan the next year. Malik’s visit, however, comes at an especially fraught moment, with the relationship essentially frozen since the brief military conflict between India and Pakistan in 2025.

In a recent development, looking ahead, a big question is whether Modi will travel to Pakistan for the SCO leaders’ summit scheduled for next August. Modi visited Pakistan in December 2015, early in his first term. Several days after his trip, Pakistani terrorists attacked an Indian Air Force base. Since that incident, Modi’s government has taken an especially hard line toward Pakistan.

Even though Jaishankar went to Pakistan in 2024, it is unlikely that Modi himself will make the trip next year—especially if the protest movement against his government that has gripped India in recent months remains active.

According to recent reports, in the Daily Mirror, writer K.K.S. Perera analyzes Sri Lanka’s new budget: “Has the 2027 Budget adequately addressed the economic difficulties confronting ordinary Sri Lankans? The answer must be examined against people’s actual living conditions rather than the Government’s financial projections, development promises, and announcements.”.

In the Print, education expert Archana Dalmia reflects on Italian-born Indian politician Sonia Gandhi’s upcoming memoir, Belonging. “Destiny had written a very different story from the one she could ever have imagined,” she writes. “Through love, loss and the unexpected turns of life, she became part of a country that was once so distant from her own.”.

In a recent development, in Dawn, public health specialist Muhammad Aftab Gohar argues the urgency of eliminating rabies in Pakistan. “The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030,” he writes. “A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.”.

According to recent reports, michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. X: @michaelkugelman.

China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
